commitResults.messageBody:
Replace the raw Task[] array + itemCount pair in Leo.java with a
TaskList that wraps an ArrayList<Task> internally, exposing add/get/
remove/size/isValidIndex. Storage.java is untouched: TaskList bridges
to its existing array-based load/save API via the new constructor and
toArray().

Behavioural change (intentional): the old hard-coded 100-task capacity
check is gone, since ArrayList grows as needed and that limit was only
ever an artifact of using a fixed-size array. Verified list can now
hold >100 tasks without error.

Verified no other behavioural change: diffed console output against
this commit's parent for an edge-case script covering empty/whitespace
arguments, malformed dates, invalid indices, and unknown commands.

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract command parsing into Parser class
commitResults.messageBody:
Move command-word/argument splitting out of Leo.java's if/else chain
into a Parser class (getCommandWord/getArguments). Leo.java now
dispatches on the parsed command word instead of using
input.startsWith(...)/input.substring(...) directly, which also let
each command collapse its 'bare word' and 'word + args' cases into a
single branch with an isEmpty() check.

Verified no behavioural change: diffed console output against this
branch's original base commit for an edge-case script covering empty/
whitespace-only arguments, malformed deadline/event formats, invalid
task numbers, and unknown commands.

commitResults.messageBody:

enforcement.

Verified: 'gradle run' produces output identical to running the

missing class- and/or method-level Javadoc (Ui, TaskList, and Parser

and public method, following se-education.org's Java conventions:
first sentence is a verb-first summary, blank line before @param/
@return/@throws, and no blank line between the doc block and the
declaration it documents. Also adds brief field comments on

commitResults.messageTitle: Tighten field visibility to match coding standard (A-CodingStandard)
commitResults.messageBody:
Audited the codebase against se-education.org's basic + intermediate
Java conventions (indentation, K&R braces, naming, no wildcard
imports, no public fields, boolean naming, etc.) - it was already
compliant on essentially every point, likely because earlier commits
this week were already written with that guide in mind.

The one real gap: Deadline.by and Event.from/to were declared
'protected' with no subclass ever relying on that access. Per the
'class variables never public' rule and general encapsulation
practice, changed both to 'private', since Task already exposes what
subclasses need via getType()/getDescription()/toFileString()/
toString() rather than direct field access.

Verified: recompiled and reran the standard regression script;
output is identical (field-visibility-only change).

commitResults.messageTitle: Use varargs for multi-line Ui messages (A-Varargs)
commitResults.messageBody:
Change Ui.showMessage(String) to Ui.showMessage(String...), so a
command that needs to display several related lines (e.g. "task
added" + the task + the new task count) can do it in one call
instead of two or three separate ones. A single-argument call still
behaves exactly as before, since Java wraps one argument into a
one-element array automatically, so no other call site needed to
change.

Applied it at every genuine multi-line call site: showWelcome,
showGoodbye, and the todo/deadline/event/mark/unmark/delete command
handlers in Leo. The dynamic-length cases (list, find) are left as
loops, since varargs doesn't help when the number of lines isn't
known until runtime.

Verified behavior-preserving by running an identical scripted command
sequence (covering every command, including error cases) against this
build and the pre-A-Varargs build and diffing the console output -
identical.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add a JavaFX GUI (Level-10)
commitResults.messageBody:
Add a graphical front end on top of the existing command logic,
following the SE-EDU JavaFX tutorial's structure
(se-education.org/guides/tutorials/javaFxPart1.html):

- Launcher: separate launch() entry point, so running from the
  packaged jar doesn't hit the "can't find JavaFX runtime" problem
  that can happen when the Application subclass is the direct
  entry point.
- Main: the actual javafx.application.Application - loads
  MainWindow.fxml and shows the window.
- MainWindow (view/MainWindow.fxml): the window itself - a
  scrollable chat log, a text field, and a Send button. Turns each
  command into a pair of DialogBox rows (what the user typed, and
  Leo's reply) and auto-scrolls to the newest one.
- DialogBox (view/DialogBox.fxml): one row of the chat log - a
  circular avatar next to a speech-bubble label, mirrored for
  Leo's replies vs. the user's own messages.
- resources/images/DaUser.png, DaLeo.png: simple generated
  placeholder avatars (solid-colour circles with a letter) - swap
  these for real artwork whenever you like, nothing else needs to
  change.

The harder part of this increment is that the GUI needs to reuse
Leo's existing command-handling logic instead of duplicating it, so:

- Leo is refactored from a static main()-only class into a normal
  instance class. main() now just does `new Leo().run()`. All the
  command-handling code that used to live directly in main()'s
  while-loop is now in a private processCommand(input, outputUi)
  method, used by both run() (the console loop) and the new
  getResponse(input) method (used by the GUI).
- Ui gains a `protected void print(String)` method that
  showMessage/showWelcome/showGoodbye all funnel through, and a new
  subclass, GuiUi, overrides just that one method to collect the
  text into a String instead of printing it. This is what lets
  getResponse(input) reuse processCommand unchanged and get back a
  String, rather than duplicating the whole command-handling
  if/else chain a second time for the GUI.
- Ui's Scanner is now created lazily (on first readCommand() call)
  rather than in the constructor, since GuiUi never calls
  readCommand() and previously would have opened a pointless
  Scanner on System.in for every single GUI reply.

The console chat loop still works exactly as before (Leo.main /
Leo.run) - I kept it rather than deleting it, since the course page
only says you no longer *need* to keep it, not that you should
remove it, and AGENTS.md asks me to avoid changing behavior that
isn't asked for. `gradle run` and the packaged jar now launch the
GUI (leo.Launcher) by default though, per the tutorial's own
build.gradle changes; see the build.gradle comments for how to run
the console version instead.

Verified behavior-preserving for the parts I *could* run here: the
console chat loop (Leo.run(), via Leo.main) still produces
byte-identical output to the pre-Level-10 build against the same
scripted command sequence used for previous increments, and I
exercised getResponse(...) directly (bypassing the GUI, which needs
JavaFX) against a range of commands including two error cases (bad
task number, unknown keyword) and confirmed each reply matches what
the console version would have printed for the same command, with
no leftover System.out output.

Caveat: I could not compile or run the actual GUI classes
(Launcher/Main/MainWindow/DialogBox) or the FXML in this sandbox,
since Maven Central is blocked here and the JavaFX artifacts aren't
available - I wrote and reviewed them very carefully against the
tutorial's own structure and proofread them by hand (no tabs/
trailing whitespace/long lines, XML is well-formed), but this is
the one piece of this batch that is genuinely untested. Please run
`gradle run` yourself and tell me what happens - if anything breaks
I'll fix it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch-A-CheckStyle for A-CheckStyle
Merge branch-Level-10 for Level-10
Merge branch-A-Varargs for A-Varargs
commitResults.messageBody:
Real merge conflict, as expected: Level-10 restructured Leo.java
(static main() -> instance class with run()/getResponse()/
processCommand()) at the same time A-Varargs consolidated
Ui.showMessage() call sites and changed Ui.showMessage's signature
to varargs - both branches touched almost the same lines of
Leo.java and Ui.java, for different reasons.

Resolved by keeping Level-10's structure (processCommand(input,
outputUi), shared by run() and getResponse()) and applying
A-Varargs' consolidation on top of it: every multi-line
outputUi.showMessage(...) call site in processCommand (todo,
deadline, event, mark, unmark, delete) now makes one varargs call
instead of two or three separate ones, same as A-Varargs did to the
original main(). Ui.showMessage is the varargs version, implemented
by looping over Level-10's `print(String)` hook rather than calling
System.out.println directly, so GuiUi's override of print() still
intercepts every line correctly regardless of whether a caller uses
the single- or multi-argument form.

Verified behavior-preserving after resolving: recompiled everything
except the (JavaFX-only, still uncompilable here) GUI classes, reran
the same scripted command sequence used throughout this batch
against the merged build and diffed it against the pre-A-CheckStyle
baseline - identical - and reran the getResponse(...) spot checks
from the Level-10 commit, which also came back identical.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add mac-aarch64/linux-aarch64 JavaFX classifiers
commitResults.messageBody:
Fixes: running the GUI on Apple Silicon (M1/M2/M3/M4) failed at
startup with "java.lang.RuntimeException: Error initializing
QuantumRenderer: no suitable pipeline found", instead of opening a
window.

Cause: the JavaFX dependencies added in Level-10 only declared win/
mac/linux classifiers. "mac" specifically means Intel-Mac native
binaries; on an Apple Silicon machine those don't match the running
CPU architecture, so JavaFX's native graphics library fails to load
and it can't find any usable rendering pipeline.

Fix: add the mac-aarch64 classifier alongside mac (and linux-aarch64
alongside linux, for the same reason, e.g. Raspberry Pi/ARM cloud
VMs - not needed for this course, but free to include). Having both
architectures' jars on the classpath at once is harmless: JavaFX's
native-library loader picks whichever one actually matches the
machine it's running on at runtime and ignores the rest.

commitResults.messageTitle: Fix DialogBox.fxml to use fx:root, not a plain <HBox> tag
commitResults.messageBody:
Fixes: launching the GUI failed with
"javafx.fxml.LoadException: Root value already specified" in
DialogBox.fxml, followed by a NullPointerException on
this.dialog.setText(...) (dialog was never injected, since the load
had already failed).

Cause: DialogBox.java's constructor calls fxmlLoader.setRoot(this) -
telling the loader "the root object already exists (the DialogBox
being constructed), configure it from this file rather than creating
a new one." But the FXML's root element was a plain <HBox ...> tag,
which tells the loader the opposite: create a brand new HBox to be
the root. Both can't be true at once, hence the conflict.

Fix: use <fx:root type="javafx.scene.layout.HBox" ...> as the root
element instead of <HBox ...>, with a matching </fx:root> close tag.
fx:root is FXML's way of saying "the root is supplied externally";
its type attribute tells the loader what class to expect so it can
still resolve the alignment/padding attributes and <children> against
it. This is the standard pattern for a custom Node subclass that is
both its own controller and its own root (as opposed to MainWindow,
where FXMLLoader creates the root itself via fx:controller, so no
fx:root is needed there).

Confirmed via the real error trace the user hit on their machine
(Apple Silicon Mac, IntelliJ, `gradle --refresh-dependencies run`)
after the previous mac-aarch64 fix resolved the earlier
QuantumRenderer error - this is a genuine bug in the FXML itself, not
an environment issue, so I could not have caught it without seeing
that trace (JavaFX still isn't runnable in this sandbox).

commitResults.messageTitle: Add Shadow plugin to bundle JavaFX into the packaged JAR (Week 5 Task 1)
commitResults.messageBody:
The plain `jar` task only ever packaged Leo's own classes, so a JAR
built with it could not run standalone once Level-10 added a real
JavaFX runtime dependency - it would fail with NoClassDefFoundError on
a computer without JavaFX installed separately. Adding the Shadow
plugin (com.gradleup.shadow, as recommended by the course's Gradle
tutorial at se-education.org/guides/tutorials/gradle.html) and its
shadowJar task produces a "fat" JAR that bundles JavaFX's classes
directly, so `gradle clean shadowJar` now produces a JAR
(build/libs/leo.jar) that runs anywhere JavaFX isn't preinstalled. The
plain `jar` task is disabled (not removed) rather than left to clash
with shadowJar's default output name.

commitResults.messageTitle: Document TaskList and Storage assumptions with assertions (A-Assertions)
commitResults.messageBody:
Several places rely on assumptions that are never written down:
TaskList.get()/remove() assumes a valid index; the TaskList
constructor assumes count fits the array; Storage.loadTasks() assumes
the save file has no more lines than the array has room for;
Leo.parseTaskNumber() assumes it will only ever return a positive
number.

Left unstated, a violation of any of these (caused by a bug elsewhere)
would surface as some unrelated exception with no clue which
assumption broke - hard to trace back to the real cause.

Let's add assert statements at all four points.

Chose assert over LeoException because these guard against bugs in
our own code, not bad user input, and using it here would treat a
"should never happen" bug as normal control flow. Chose assert over a
comment because an assertion is actively checked by the JVM during
development, not just read (or ignored) by a human.

Ran the same commands with and without -ea; output was identical both
times, confirming the assertions never fire during normal use.

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract per-command handler methods from processCommand (A-CodeQuality)
commitResults.messageBody:
processCommand's body contains the full logic for every command -
roughly 220 lines in one long if-else chain.

This makes the method hard to read: finding out what one command does
means skimming past every other command's logic first, and no
command's logic can be tested, or changed independently of the
others.

Splitting each command's logic into its own method would let
processCommand's own job - dispatching to the right command - be
visible at a glance, while keeping each command's logic self-contained
and easy to find.

Let's extract each command's logic out of processCommand into its own
private handler method (e.g. handleMark, handleTodo, handleDeadline),
leaving processCommand itself as a short dispatch table that calls
the matching handler.

A handler method per command is used here, rather than just
converting the if-else chain into a switch statement, because a
switch alone would still leave every command's logic in the same
method - splitting into separate methods is what actually lets each
one be read, tested, or changed on its own.

Verified behavior-preserving by comparing console output for the same
scripted command sequence before and after the change; output was
identical in both cases.

commitResults.messageTitle: Use Streams for filtering and formatting task lists (A-Streams)
commitResults.messageBody:
TaskList.find() and Leo's "list"/"find" commands build their output
with manual loops: one filters tasks by keyword, the other two loop
over an index to number each task for display.

Which tasks to keep, and the number to attach to each one, is spread
across loop headers, counter variables, and accumulator lists, rather
than being visible directly in the code.

Java's Streams API expresses filtering and numbering directly, so the
code can say what it's doing rather than how to loop through it.

Let's replace the loop in TaskList.find() with a filtering stream, and
replace the indexed display loops with a stream that pairs each task
with its display number directly.

A stream that generates each task's display number directly is used
here, because it keeps each task tied to its number without any extra
mutable state to track.

Verified behavior-preserving by comparing console output for the same
scripted command sequence before and after the change; output was
identical in both cases.

commitResults.messageTitle: Highlight error replies and keep focus in the input field (A-BetterGui)
commitResults.messageBody:
Every one of Leo's replies - a successful 'task added' confirmation
and 'that task number does not exist' alike - looked exactly the same
in the chat log: same bubble, same colour, same everything. Nothing
made an error stand out from a normal reply, so a mistake (a bad date
format, a typo'd command) was easy to miss, especially scrolling back
through a longer conversation. The text field also lost focus after
every command, so sending several commands in a row meant re-clicking
into it each time.

Let's add a small Reply type - the reply text plus whether it was an
error - and a new Ui.showError(String) (GuiUi overrides it to record
that an error happened; the console Ui just falls back to its existing
showMessage behaviour, since the console has no such distinction to
make). Leo.processCommand's three error-producing catch blocks
(LeoException, IOException, DateTimeParseException) now call
showError instead of showMessage - no change to what they say, only
that GuiUi now notices. A new Leo.getReply(String) exposes this to
callers; the existing getResponse(String) becomes a thin wrapper
around it (getReply(input).getText()), so every existing caller and
test keeps working unchanged. DialogBox.getLeoDialog now takes that
error flag and applies a light red background/border/text style to
error bubbles, leaving every other bubble exactly as before. Also let
MainWindow.handleUserInput call userInput.requestFocus() after
clearing the field, so the caret stays put for the next command.

An alternative would have been to detect errors by pattern-matching
the reply text in the GUI layer (e.g. checking for known phrases) -
rejected, since that's fragile (an error message wording changing
anywhere would silently break the highlighting) and duplicates
knowledge processCommand's catch blocks already have for free.

Main/Launcher/MainWindow/DialogBox, which need JavaFX on the classpath
that isn't available in this sandbox) exercising Leo.getReply()/
Ui.showError()/GuiUi.isError() directly: a failing command (empty
todo, an unknown command, a bad date) is flagged as an error, a
successful one is not, and getResponse() still returns exactly the
text getReply().getText() would - so nothing already relying on
getResponse() changes behaviour. DialogBox.java and MainWindow.java
themselves were checked by hand rather than compiled (no JavaFX/Gradle
network access here) - their changes are small, mechanical uses of
standard JavaFX APIs (Node#setStyle, Node#requestFocus), so please
run this branch's GUI for real ('gradle run' or via the IDE) before
merging, to confirm the error styling and focus behaviour actually
look right.

commitResults.messageTitle: Handle more user errors and environmental edge cases (A-MoreErrorHandling)
commitResults.messageBody:
Leo's constructor loaded saved tasks into a Task[100] array that
Storage.loadTasks(Task[]) then filled up to its length - a save file
with more than 100 non-blank lines silently overran that array with
an unguarded ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, crashing Leo on startup.
TaskList itself has never had a capacity limit (see
TaskListTest#canHoldMoreThanOneHundredTasks), so this was purely an
artifact of how the loading path allocated its buffer, not a real
constraint - a save file reaching 100 tasks is easily reached after a
few weeks of normal use.

Two commands (deadline, event) also silently misparsed a repeated
delimiter instead of rejecting it: 'deadline return book /by mon /by
tue' split on only the first '/by', so the second one ended up folded
into the due-time field and surfaced as a generic date-format error
with no hint of the real mistake. And adding a task identical to one
already on the list succeeded with no acknowledgement at all, even
though it is very likely a slip (e.g. re-running the same 'todo ...'
command twice).

Let's fix the loading path by having Storage.loadTasks() return a
List<Task> sized to exactly what was loaded, instead of populating a
caller-supplied fixed-size array - this removes the capacity mismatch
(and the assumption it depended on) rather than just raising the
limit. Let's also add Parser.hasDuplicateDelimiter(), used by
handleDeadline/handleEvent to reject a repeated '/by', '/from', or
'/to' with a message that names the actual problem, and
TaskList.containsSimilar()/Task.isSameTaskAs(), used to append a
non-blocking warning line when an added task duplicates an existing
one (chosen over rejecting it outright, since a repeated task is
occasionally intentional, e.g. a recurring reminder).

An alternative for the loading fix would have been to just raise the
fixed array's capacity (e.g. to 1000) - rejected, since that still
leaves a silent crash for anyone who eventually exceeds whatever
number is picked, only postponing the same bug rather than removing
it.

Verified via a manual smoke-test harness (javac + a small driver
calling Leo.getResponse() directly, since this sandbox has no network
access to Gradle's plugin portal or Maven Central to run the project's
own Gradle/JUnit setup): loading a save file with 150 tasks no longer
crashes and lists all 150; 'deadline'/'event' commands with a
duplicate '/by', '/from', or '/to' are rejected with the new specific
message while single-delimiter commands still succeed unchanged;
adding a duplicate task appends the new warning line while a distinct
task does not; and the existing add/mark/list/find/delete flow is
unaffected. TaskList's and Task's public APIs used by the existing
JUnit tests (TaskListTest, TaskTest, ParserTest) were only added to,
never changed, so those tests are unaffected by this commit.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add tests for Storage, LeoException, command dispatch, and new task-equality logic (A-MoreTesting)
commitResults.messageBody:
TaskListTest, TaskTest, and ParserTest already covered TaskList,
Task/Todo/Deadline/Event, and Parser's command-word/argument
splitting - but Storage (save-file loading/saving, malformed-line
handling), LeoException (the checked exception every command handler
throws), and Leo itself (command dispatch - the if-else chain in
processCommand that every user-facing behaviour ultimately runs
through) had no tests at all, and the new A-MoreErrorHandling
behaviour (duplicate-delimiter rejection, duplicate-task warnings,
loading past the old fixed-100 capacity) had none either.

Let's add StorageTest (load/save round-tripping all three task types,
blank lines skipped, malformed/unknown-type lines throwing
IOException, and a regression test loading 150 tasks - guarding
against the fixed-100-capacity bug A-MoreErrorHandling just fixed) and
LeoExceptionTest (message preserved, is a checked exception). Let's
also add LeoTest, driving Leo the same way the GUI does - through
getResponse() - since processCommand and every handleXxx method are
private and only reachable that way; it covers each command's happy
path and error path, including the new duplicate-delimiter and
duplicate-task-warning behaviour, and confirms tasks persist across
Leo instances (i.e. that the constructor and save-on-every-mutation
behaviour actually work together end to end, not just in isolation).
Finally, extend TaskTest with Deadline/Event invalid-date-format
coverage and Task.isSameTaskAs (added by A-MoreErrorHandling, so
untested until now), and ParserTest with
Parser.hasDuplicateDelimiter.

Storage and Leo both read/write the fixed path data/leo.txt relative
to the working directory - there's no way to point them elsewhere -
so StorageTest and LeoTest each back up whatever is already at that
path in @BeforeEach and restore it in @AfterEach, rather than risking
a stray developer save file getting overwritten by running the test
suite.

An alternative for testing command dispatch would have been to give
each handleXxx method package-private visibility and test them
directly - rejected, since that would mean changing production-code
visibility purely to make it more testable, and getResponse() already
exercises the exact same code path a real user's input does, which is
a more faithful test regardless.

Verified with a small local test harness (javac against a minimal
stub of the org.junit.jupiter.api annotations/assertions actually
used, plus a reflection-based runner invoking every @Test method) -
not full Gradle/JUnit, since this sandbox has no network access to
either the Gradle plugin portal or Maven Central: all 60 tests across
all six test classes (the 3 pre-existing plus the 3 new ones) pass,
confirming nothing here changes the pre-existing tests' behaviour.
Also checked by hand against config/checkstyle/checkstyle.xml (import
order/grouping, Javadoc tag order and presence, line length, no
tabs/trailing whitespace) so 'gradle check' should pass unmodified
when run for real.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge pull request #7 from samairakapur/branch-A-MoreTesting
Merge pull request #8 from samairakapur/branch-A-BetterGui
Add a warmer theme, quick-action buttons, and personality (A-BetterGui follow-up)
commitResults.messageBody:
The GUI worked but looked and felt bare: plain default JavaFX styling
with no colour distinction between the user's own messages and Leo's
replies, a flat one-line greeting, and every command had to be typed
out from memory with the exact syntax (delimiters included).

Let's add a small stylesheet (theme.css, loaded once on the Scene in
Main.java) giving the window a warm off-white background and
colour-coding chat bubbles by sender - a soft blue for the user, a
soft green for Leo - via new .user-bubble/.leo-bubble style classes
DialogBox now applies based on a new isUser constructor parameter.
DialogBox's existing inline error-reply styling is untouched and still
takes priority over these, since JavaFX applies inline styles after
stylesheet rules.

Let's also add a row of quick-action buttons (List, Todo, Deadline,
Event, Bye) below the chat log. List/Bye need no further input, so
clicking them sends the command immediately through the exact same
handleUserInput() path as pressing Enter (MainWindow#submitCommand);
Todo/Deadline/Event need the user's own details, so clicking them
instead fills the text field with a ready-to-edit template - for
Deadline/Event, with the DESCRIPTION placeholder pre-selected so
typing immediately replaces it - and focuses the field
(MainWindow#prefillCommand), rather than guessing at arguments on the
user's behalf. The window's minimum height (both in the FXML and in
Main.java, which must agree) moves from 220 to 260 to keep this new
row from ever being clipped.

Finally, a bit of personality: Leo's console and GUI greetings, and
its goodbye, are warmer now, and every successful todo/deadline/event
addition ends with one of five rotating friendly lines
(Leo#pickFlourish). None of the existing required wording changed or
moved - flourishes are appended as an extra line after it - since
LeoTest (from branch-A-MoreTesting) checks this text with
String#contains, not equality, so this stays compatible with that
branch's tests regardless of merge order.

One thing to flag for when you merge this alongside
branch-A-MoreErrorHandling: both branches modify the same three
handleTodo/handleDeadline/handleEvent methods in Leo.java (that branch
wraps them with duplicate-task detection and a shared confirmation
helper; this one adds the flourish line), so merging the second one in
will very likely hit a real conflict there - happy to help resolve it
the same way we did for the A-Streams/A-CodeQuality conflict earlier,
once you're at that point.

Verified with a small local driver (javac against every file except
Main/Launcher/MainWindow/DialogBox, which need JavaFX unavailable in
this sandbox): 40 repeated todo commands all still contain the
required confirmation text regardless of which flourish was appended,
and more than one distinct flourish actually appeared; the goodbye
message still contains the required line plus the new one. As before,
MainWindow.fxml/DialogBox.fxml/DialogBox.java/MainWindow.java/Main.java
themselves were checked by hand (validated as well-formed XML, and
reviewed line-by-line against known JavaFX APIs) rather than compiled,
so please actually run this for real before merging - the styling and
the quick-action buttons in particular are worth clicking through.
